By analyzing current barriers to deployment, including workflow integration and regulatory hurdles, this article argues that although artificial intelligence holds transformative potential for musculoskeletal radiology, its success depends on moving beyond narrow diagnostic tasks toward robust multi-institutional validation, to evolve from a speculative trend into an essential clinical copilot tool.

records.title: Application of Language Models for the Analysis of Adverse Drug Events in Pharmaceutical Research and Development: Scoping Review.

content.title: Application of Language Models for the Analysis of Adverse Drug Events in Pharmaceutical Research and Development: Scoping Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Adverse drug events (ADEs) remain a critical safety issue in pharmaceutical research and development (Pharma R&D), necessitating robust methods for early detection and surveillance. Language models (LMs) are increasingly used in ADE analysis, addressing safety challenges during drug development and postmarket surveillance. Language modeling approaches, ranging from static embeddings to large language models (LLMs), capitalize on diverse data sources, such as clinical trial datasets, electronic health records, and social media posts, to predict ADEs, analyze real-world evidence, and improve drug screening and pharmacovigilance systems.

Objective

This scoping review aims to map the application of LMs for the analysis of ADEs across the Pharma R&D lifecycle.

Methods

Following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for relevant papers published between January 2015 and October 2025.

Results

This review identified 49 relevant papers. Overall, LM applications in Pharma R&D safety analysis are concentrated in 2 distinct phases: ADE prediction during the premarket phase (n=16) and ADE detection in postmarket surveillance (n=33).

Conclusions

While some models demonstrate high predictive performance, persistent challenges, including data heterogeneity and limited external validation, hinder widespread adoption. Despite these barriers, discriminative and generative LMs have the potential to transform drug safety across the pre- and postapproval phases, especially when integrated with real-world pharmacovigilance frameworks.

records.title: AI-Guided Histopathological and Molecular Phenotyping of Salivary Glands in Sjögren's Disease: Subtyping, Mechanistic Insights, and Translational Implications-A Systematic Review and Structured Functional Synthesis.

content.title: AI-Guided Histopathological and Molecular Phenotyping of Salivary Glands in Sjögren's Disease: Subtyping, Mechanistic Insights, and Translational Implications-A Systematic Review and Structured Functional Synthesis.
content.abstract:
Background/objectives

Salivary-gland biopsy is central to Sjögren's disease (SjD) assessment, but conventional measures incompletely capture glandular heterogeneity. This systematic review evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) applications to SjD salivary-gland histopathology and molecular profiling, including biological and translational validation.

Methods

PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched. Eligible studies used salivary-gland tissue as the primary analytical substrate or provided substantive glandular validation of systemic AI/ML findings. Evidence was synthesized functionally because of methodological heterogeneity.

Results

Twenty-five studies were included. AI/ML identified histopathological and molecular phenotypes spanning immune/interferon activation, tissue architecture and immune-cell organization, epithelial stress and metabolic/cell-death remodeling, and translational response. Only a limited subset progressed beyond computational or tissue-level confirmation to functional perturbation, pharmacological testing, in vivo validation, or human treatment-response assessment. Recurrent public-dataset reuse, small cohorts, heterogeneous pipelines, and limited independent validation constrained reproducibility.

Conclusions

AI/ML supports multidimensional SjD glandular phenotyping and shows emerging translational potential, but demonstrated clinical or therapeutic utility remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter validation is required before AI-derived glandular phenotypes can inform routine patient stratification or therapeutic decision-making.

records.title: Effects of Multicomponent Digital Health Interventions on Multidimensional Physical Activity in Older Adults: Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression of Randomized Controlled Trials.

content.title: Effects of Multicomponent Digital Health Interventions on Multidimensional Physical Activity in Older Adults: Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression of Randomized Controlled Trials.
content.abstract:
Background

The comprehensive effects of multicomponent digital health interventions (DHIs) on multidimensional physical activity indicators and sedentary behavior (SB) remain controversial.

Objective

This systematic review aimed to evaluate the impact of multicomponent DHIs on daily steps, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), light physical activity, total physical activity, and SB in older adults.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, The Cochrane Library, and CINAHL were searched up to February 20, 2026. Randomized controlled trials concerning multicomponent DHIs for promoting exercise behavior in older adults were included. RoB 2.0 was used to evaluate study quality. Meta-analyses were performed using the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman random-effects model, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were calculated via Nagashima adjustment to evaluate effect dispersion. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) system was used to evaluate evidence certainty.

Results

A total of 26 randomized controlled trials (n=4129) were included. The results showed that multicomponent DHIs significantly improved daily steps (mean difference [MD] 822.8, 95% CI 198.3 to 1447.3 steps/d; 95% PI -1452.4 to 3098.0) and MVPA (MD 45.9, 95% CI 23.9 to 67.9 min/wk; 95% PI -9.4 to 101.2). However, the improvements in SB (MD -283.7, 95% CI -610.8 to 43.5 min/wk; 95% PI -984.5 to 417.1), total physical activity (MD 104.4; 95% CI -109.2 to 318.0 min/wk; 95% PI -444.4 to 653.2), and light physical activity (MD 39.3, 95% CI -96.2 to 174.7 min/wk; 95% PI -227.6 to 306.2) did not reach statistical significance. As some included studies combined digital tools with human support, the independent contribution of digital technology remains uncertain. PIs indicated a certain degree of dispersion across different clinical contexts. Subgroup analysis showed higher effect sizes for standalone wearables, human-assisted interventions, and populations with chronic disease risks. Meta-regression showed that effect sizes remained stable across different ages and durations. The trim-and-fill method confirmed the robustness of MVPA results. GRADE assessment indicated "moderate" certainty for MVPA and "low" for daily steps and other indicators.

Conclusions

This systematic review suggests that multicomponent DHIs may serve as an effective means for enhancing daily steps and MVPA in older adults. The innovation lies in evaluating the true effect distribution of multicomponent DHIs through Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman random-effects models and Nagashima PIs. Compared with previous studies, this review identified the impact of population characteristics and control group differences on effect estimates using PI and subgroup models, confirming that advanced age did not significantly diminish the good adaptability of older adults to DHIs. Evidence limitations include high heterogeneity, lack of long-term follow-up, and differences between objective and subjective measurement tools. In practice, priority should be given to hardware carriers with simplified interaction and integrated human support, with tailored strategies developed for different risk subgroups.

records.title: Implications and risk of new versus persisting intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms after pancreatic surgery: meta-analysis.

content.title: Implications and risk of new versus persisting intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms after pancreatic surgery: meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Interpretation of recurrence following resection of intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) is hindered by inconsistent terminology and outcome reporting. A distinction between metachronous/de novo IPMN development, progression of residual disease, and true recurrence of invasive entities is rarely considered.

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA and Cochrane guidelines (PROSPERO-ID: 1009399). The primary endpoint was postoperative recurrence of non-invasive IPMN and IPMN-derived pancreatic cancer (PC). Recurrence following resection of non-invasive IPMN was reclassified as progression of persistent cysts or de novo metachronous IPMN. Secondary endpoints comprised risk-factors for recurrence.

Results

Sixty-six articles with 11 464 patients were included. After a median follow-up of 26 (interquartile range (i.q.r.) 18.0-53.0) to 72 (i.q.r. 5-318) months, the recurrence rate of IPMN-derived PC was 41.9% (1646/3925 patients), with a 5-year pooled recurrence-free survival of 46.6%. Systemic recurrence was most common (1034/1646; 62.8%), followed by locoregional (430/1646; 26.1%). Secondary treatments were administered in 655/1646 patients (39.8%) presenting with recurrence and included chemotherapy (65.5%), surgery (22.1%) and radiation (5.8%). Lymph node involvement (hazard ratio 2.87, 95% confidence interval 1.51 to 5.43) and tubular subtype (hazard ratio 1.68, 1.16 to 2.43) were identified as independent predictors of recurrence-free survival. The overall recurrence rate following pancreatic resection of non-invasive IPMN was 11.2% (831/7446), after median follow-up of 28 (i.q.r. 1-153) to 114 (i.q.r. 12-204) months. Among these, 408 (49.1%) developed as de novo lesions in the remnant pancreas and 174 (20.9%) as progression of pre-existing cyst detected at the time of index surgery; the remaining 249 patients (30.0%) could not be reclassified. Non-invasive recurrence was more common (308; 37.1%) than IPMN-derived PC (118; 14.2%), whereas the type of recurrence was unspecified in 405 patients (48.7%). Secondary treatment data were available for 265 patients, of whom 131 (49.4%) underwent reoperation.

Conclusion

The recurrence rate of IPMN-derived PC is high and warrants close surveillance policies. The majority of 'recurring' non-invasive IPMNs are de novo lesions. Standardized reporting, distinguishing true recurrence from de novo development and progression of residual disease, is essential to stratify recurrence risk and optimize surveillance protocols accurately.

records.title: Artificial intelligence tools in dermatology education: A scoping review on their application, efficacy, and limitations.
records.publisher: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore

content.title: Artificial intelligence tools in dermatology education: A scoping review on their application, efficacy, and limitations.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly explored for medical education, and dermatology, with its visual diagnostic focus, holds promise for AIenhanced learning. However, evidence on its educational effectiveness remains limited and fragmented. This scoping review aimed to assess the evidence base for applications and limitations of AI-based educational tools in dermatology.

Method

A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and PsycINFO up to July 2025 was conducted. Data were synthesised narratively, considering types of AI interventions and their assessed outcomes. These were analysed with the Cost, Usability, Credibility, Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, Explainability (CUC-FATE) framework. Study quality was assessed with ROBINS-I and a COSMIN-informed checklist.

Results

A total of 827 records were screened, with 360 duplicates removed, yielding 467 studies. Six full-length studies and 1 conference abstract met inclusion criteria, mostly from 2023 to 2025. These explored AI-generated clinical images, Large Language Model-generated vignettes, intelligent tutoring systems, and clinical decision support tools. Content validation studies generally reported favourable ratings for accuracy, clarity, and educational utility, while intervention studies suggested possible benefits for learning performance and diagnostic accuracy. Usability and credibility were commonly assessed, whereas cost, accountability, fairness, transparency, and explainability were rarely examined.

Conclusion

Most of the studies reviewed had high risk of bias, small sample sizes, and limited methodological rigour, with significant heterogeneity in examined educational outcomes limiting synthesis. While current initial studies on AI hold promise, this scoping review underscores the need for more robust studies with standardised evaluation frameworks, prioritising ethical principles such as fairness, explainability, and accountability for safe integration in training.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy combined with tyrosine kinase inhibitors and PD-1 inhibitors for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy and safety of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy combined with tyrosine kinase inhibitors and PD-1 inhibitors for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

The triplet combination of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC), a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), and a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) inhibitor has emerged as a highly promising strategy for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (uHCC). This study aimed to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy and safety of this triple-therapy compared with the dual-therapy of a TKI plus a PD-1 inhibitor.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials or comparative cohort studies that assessed HAIC plus a TKI and a PD-1 inhibitor (H-T-P) versus a TKI plus a PD-1 inhibitor (T-P) for uHCC. The primary endpoints were overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), and disease control rate (DCR). The secondary endpoint was treatment-related adverse events (AEs). A random-effects model was employed to pool data, calculating hazard ratios (HRs) or relative risks (RRs) with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results

A total of 12 studies involving 2,386 patients with uHCC were included. Compared with T-P dual therapy, the H-T-P triple therapy was associated with significantly improved OS (HR, 0.51; 95%CI, 0.47-0.56; P < 0.001) and PFS (HR, 0.59; 95%CI, 0.51-0.68; P < 0.001). Furthermore, the H-T-P group demonstrated a significantly higher ORR (RR, 1.97; 95%CI, 1.73-2.24; P < 0.001) and DCR (RR, 1.19; 95%CI, 1.11-1.28; P < 0.001). Regarding safety, while no significant difference was observed in the overall incidence of all-grade AEs (P = 0.238), the incidence of grade ≥3 AEs was significantly higher in the triple-therapy arm (RR, 1.29; 95%CI, 1.13-1.48; P = 0.004), consisting primarily of manageable hepatotoxicity and hematologic toxicities.

Conclusion

Our findings indicate that for patients with uHCC, the H-T-P triple-therapy regimen is superior to dual therapy in terms of survival benefits and tumor response. The associated increase in severe toxicity is considered predictable and clinically manageable.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420251113276.

records.title: Identification of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal targets utilizing artificial intelligence-driven precision medicine.

content.title: Identification of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal targets utilizing artificial intelligence-driven precision medicine.
content.abstract: Cancer metabolism is highly plastic, and most attempts to turn that plasticity into a therapeutic target fail for a specific, recurring reason: a computational prediction of a metabolic vulnerability is not the same evidentiary object as an experimentally confirmed one, and the two are routinely discussed as if they were interchangeable. This review takes that distinction as its starting point rather than its conclusion. Artificial intelligence and genome-scale systems biology have made it easy to generate metabolic hypotheses at a scale no experimental program could match - machine learning models trained on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data now output candidate vulnerabilities, biomarkers, and drug combinations faster than they can be tested - but the resulting literature has not been consistently honest about how far any given prediction has actually traveled toward clinical relevance. We examine six areas where this gap is most visible: multi-omics data integration, genome-scale metabolic network modeling, computational discovery of metabolic vulnerabilities and synthetic lethal interactions, single-cell and spatial resolution of metabolic heterogeneity, AI-guided drug and biomarker discovery, and the small set of studies that have actually reached clinical testing. Rather than summarizing these areas as separate literatures, we grade every substantive finding discussed against an explicit four-tier evidence standard - associative, mechanistic, perturbation-validated, or clinically tested - and we apply that standard critically rather than deferentially: several widely cited computational vulnerabilities remain unconfirmed outside the cell lines in which they were discovered, genome-scale models continue to carry unresolved gaps in reaction coverage that limit their predictive reach, and, of the AI-derived metabolic predictions discussed in this review, only one has so far been tested in a completed prospective clinical trial. We argue that this shortage of prospective validation, not a shortage of computational sophistication, is the field's central constraint, and we close by identifying where methodological effort would do the most good: standardized validation reporting, tissue-resolved rather than bulk metabolic models, and closer coupling between computational prediction and the specific experimental designs capable of falsifying it.

records.title: Operationalising digital and AI pathology in translational research and drug development: an infrastructure and regulatory perspective from biobank to companion diagnostic.

content.title: Operationalising digital and AI pathology in translational research and drug development: an infrastructure and regulatory perspective from biobank to companion diagnostic.
content.abstract: Digital and artificial intelligence (AI) pathology have advanced rapidly and are increasingly embedded in translational research, clinical trials and regulated diagnostic devices. Multiple reviews have addressed the underlying computational methods, oncology applications and clinical translation barriers; however, the operational and regulatory infrastructure required to deploy these technologies across the full drug-development pipeline remains under-reviewed. This structured narrative review synthesises peer-reviewed literature and regulatory documents identified through searches of PubMed, Embase and Web of Science between January 2019 and April 2026 (78 sources retained) on the end-to-end ecosystem connecting AI-ready tissue biobanks, preclinical pathology, AI-assisted patient screening, clinical-trial endpoint adjudication, central pathology review, Contract Research Organization (CRO) workflows and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulatory pathways governing In Vitro Diagnostics (IVD), Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and Companion Diagnostics (CDx). Unlike prior method-centric or oncology-clinician-centric reviews, we focus on the infrastructure between models and patients, including Laboratory Information Systems (LIS), Image Management Systems (IMS), AI orchestration and structured reporting under Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments, College of American Pathologists, Good Laboratory Practice, Good Clinical Laboratory Practice, Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act and FDA frameworks. We provide a vendor-agnostic comparison of integrated pathology platforms, a mapping of FDA regulatory pathways (510(k), De Novo, premarket approval) to digital-pathology product categories, a stage-by-stage map from each drug-development challenge to its enabling infrastructure and regulatory framework, and a critical appraisal of the unresolved bottlenecks that gate broad adoption: domain shift, interpretability, annotation cost, algorithmic bias, external validation, regulatory uncertainty and reimbursement. A governed, interoperable LIS, IMS and AI ecosystem is a prerequisite for translating digital-pathology research into regulator-grade evidence. Priorities include external validation against reporting standards (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis - Artificial Intelligence (TRIPOD-AI), Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM), Development and Early-stage Clinical Identification and Delegation Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (DECIDE-AI)), harmonisation with the EU AI Act and EU Medical Device Regulation and cost-effectiveness evaluation in real-world deployment.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency trauma perioperative management: applications, performance benchmarks, and translation barriers.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency trauma perioperative management: applications, performance benchmarks, and translation barriers.
content.abstract: This review examines the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in the perioperative management of emergency trauma. Published studies suggest performance advantages of AI over traditional methods in prehospital triage, radiographic injury detection, massive transfusion prediction, and early warning of postoperative complications, although findings vary across study designs and validation settings. However, actual adoption in trauma care remains limited due to data heterogeneity, performance degradation in external validation, workflow integration challenges, lack of interpretability, and a scarcity of prospective interventional evidence. This review further argues that methodologically inflated benchmark performance constitutes an underrecognized barrier to adoption in its own right, and that bridging the implementation gap will likely require a shift from area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)-centered reporting toward reporting sensitivity at prespecified clinical thresholds and evaluating patient outcomes in prospective interventional trials.

records.title: Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research.
records.publisher: The Indian journal of radiology & imaging

content.title: Legal and Regulatory Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Use in Medical and Radiology Research.
content.abstract:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical imaging and radiology research, improving image acquisition, interpretation, workflow efficiency, and decision support. However, its rapid adoption has introduced complex legal and regulatory challenges involving patient privacy, data governance, algorithm validation, liability, intellectual property, transparency, cybersecurity, and ethical oversight. A comprehensive understanding of the evolving legal landscape is essential for the safe, effective, and legally compliant implementation of AI in radiology.

Methods

A narrative review of the published literature and current regulatory guidance was conducted. Relevant international legal and regulatory frameworks governing AI in medical imaging were evaluated, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, General Data Protection Regulation, U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, World Health Organization recommendations, International Medical Device Regulators Forum principles, and selected national regulations. Key topics reviewed included data protection, informed consent, AI validation, regulatory approval pathways, post-market surveillance, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, explainability, and medico-legal responsibility.

Results

Current regulatory frameworks increasingly classify AI-enabled radiology software as SaMD, requiring risk-based evaluation, clinical validation, quality management systems, and continuous post-market performance monitoring. Regulatory authorities emphasize transparency, human oversight, data security, and lifecycle governance of AI systems. Nevertheless, important legal challenges remain, including liability for AI-assisted diagnostic errors, ownership of AI-generated outputs, secondary use of imaging data, cross-border data sharing, algorithmic bias, and regulation of adaptive or continuously learning AI models.

Conclusions

The legal framework governing AI in radiology is evolving in parallel with technological innovation. Responsible integration of AI into clinical practice and research requires harmonized international regulations, robust data governance, standardized validation protocols, transparent algorithm development, and clearly defined legal accountability. Continued collaboration among radiologists, researchers, regulators, policymakers, industry, and legal experts will be essential to ensure that AI technologies remain safe, ethical, equitable, and trustworthy while maximizing their potential to improve patient care.

records.title: A Case-Based Framework for Teaching Artificial Intelligence Applications in Medical Education.
records.publisher: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources

content.title: A Case-Based Framework for Teaching Artificial Intelligence Applications in Medical Education.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-based tools are emerging across many areas of medicine. The next generation of medical professionals must be prepared to critically assess the tools they will use, including how they work and the ethical or legal implications of their implementation. To address this need, we developed a generalizable case-writing framework that enables educators and learners to engage with clinical cases integrating AI/ML concepts, clinical reasoning, and ethical considerations.

Methods

We designed a case-writing template to compose clinical case scenarios that integrate clinical, technical, and ethical/legal learning objectives relating to AI applications in medicine. Medical students used this template to construct 3 cases. Student-authored cases were presented to a broader audience in 1-hour sessions: first as a pilot event, then as a class-wide lecture for 140 fourth-year medical students in a transition-into-residency course.

Results

After the sessions, student audiences had a statistically significant increase in familiarity with key AI terminology, a greater appreciation for the importance of ethical considerations of AI applications in health care, and an increased perceived importance of integrating AI-related topics into the medical curriculum.

Discussion

A case-based framework provides a scalable approach to integrating AI education into existing curricula by connecting clinical scenarios with technical concepts and the ethical considerations of AI adoption; cases offer a familiar format that helps learners understand AI applications in patient care while exploring implementation challenges. The case-writing template and 3 sample cases are provided as adaptable resources for educators seeking to incorporate AI literacy.

records.title: Integrating predictive modeling, imaging, and EHR-linked decision support in spine informatics.
records.publisher: European spine journal : official publication of the European Spine Society, the European Spinal Deformity Society, and the European Section of the Cervical Spine Research Society

content.title: Integrating predictive modeling, imaging, and EHR-linked decision support in spine informatics.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming spine care by enabling analysis of imaging, clinical, and textual data to support diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment planning. Techniques including deep learning-based image analysis, radiomics, and natural language processing (NLP) offer opportunities to standardize interpretation and derive quantitative biomarkers beyond human visual assessment. This narrative review examines recent innovations in spine-focused biomedical informatics and evaluates their clinical relevance and translational challenges.

Methods

A narrative review was conducted, focusing on AI in spine care across imaging, radiomics, NLP of electronic health records, and clinical decision support. Literature was selected via targeted PubMed searches; studies describing technical development, validation, and clinical implementation were synthesized, addressing explainability, uncertainty, workflow, and regulation.

Results

Convolutional neural networks enable vertebral and disc segmentation, detection of degenerative and traumatic pathology, and quantitative assessment of paraspinal musculature. Radiomics approaches extract high-dimensional imaging features that improve the prediction of osteoporosis, fracture risk, tumor characterization, and surgical outcomes. NLP techniques, including emerging large language models, unlock clinically relevant information from unstructured text, enhancing outcome prediction and population-level analyses. Multimodal clinical decision support systems integrating imaging, EHR data, and NLP-derived features demonstrate promise for personalized risk assessment and treatment guidance. Challenges remain regarding data heterogeneity, generalizability, privacy, and prospective validation.

Conclusion

AI-driven biomedical informatics holds substantial promise to enhance diagnostic accuracy, prognostication, and personalized decision-making in spine care. Successful clinical translation will require robust validation, explainable, uncertainty-aware models, regulatory alignment, and integration into clinical workflows to ensure safe, trustworthy, and patient-centered adoption.

records.title: Toward explainable traffic crash liability analysis via neural-symbolic multimodal reasoning: Integrating visual perception with legal knowledge graphs.

content.title: Toward explainable traffic crash liability analysis via neural-symbolic multimodal reasoning: Integrating visual perception with legal knowledge graphs.
content.abstract: Determining traffic crash liability relies on rigorous on-site evidence and legal provisions and involves substantial manual intervention and potential human error. However, intelligent traffic monitoring systems focus on detection and tracking and cannot provide structured, rule-grounded decision support for formal crash-liability analysis. Moreover, emerging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) suffer from object hallucination that distorts or omits physical evidence, and their opaque reasoning cannot produce explicit evidence-to-rule chains required for traceable and reviewable liability analysis. This paper proposes CrashLex, an explainable neural-symbolic decision-support framework that integrates visual perception with legal knowledge graph reasoning to align multimodal inference with predefined statutory rules and traceability requirements. Within CrashLex, a dual-query vision-language architecture employs parallel semantic and symbolic streams to mitigate object hallucination, utilizing Scene Queries for global context modeling and Perception Queries for fine-grained atomic feature extraction, respectively. The domain-specific legal knowledge graph maps these atomic facts from observable physical conditions to corresponding statutory elements, providing a structured basis for rule-grounded assessment. A logic-driven aggregation protocol then imposes explicit constraints derived from extracted facts and statutory provisions onto the inference process, thereby enabling traceable and interpretable preliminary liability assessment. On the held-out DeepAccident benchmark, CrashLex achieves a Legal Accuracy of 94.0% under the fixed legal-output evaluation protocol and an Object Hallucination Rate of 2.8%, corresponding to an 82.1% relative reduction from the 15.6% rate of the best-performing MLLM baseline on this metric. CrashLex grounds its assessment results in the deterministic execution of predefined legal rules rather than relying solely on unconstrained probabilistic generation, providing verifiable reasoning chains for rule-grounded human review.

records.title: Legal challenges and regulatory responses in online medical consultation.

content.title: Legal challenges and regulatory responses in online medical consultation.
content.abstract: Online medical consultation (OMC), a component of digital health, has expanded rapidly, giving rise to a variety of operational models. Furthermore, advances in artificial intelligence have created new opportunities for its evolution. With their abundant medical resources and technological capabilities, major cities such as Beijing have experienced particularly rapid growth in OMC. However, given the lack of OMC-specific regulations, the sector in Beijing still faces several legal uncertainties, notably regarding the legal status of OMC services and platform liability. Therefore, it is recommended that cities such as Beijing establish a dedicated OMC regulatory framework centered on comprehensive local departmental rules. Such rules can define the nature of services and platform liability under the overarching principle that standards should be tailored to the operational model.

records.title: Harnessing single-cell omics for farmed animal improvement and human health.
records.publisher: Journal of animal science and biotechnology

content.title: Harnessing single-cell omics for farmed animal improvement and human health.
content.abstract: Cellular heterogeneity underlies the regulation of complex traits and diseases, making cell-resolved molecular characterization fundamental for advancing precision agriculture and human biomedicine. Rapid advances in single-cell omics technologies, together with the ever-evolving computational methods, have led to the establishment of large-scale single cell atlases across multiple species, providing unprecedented opportunities to systematically dissect cellular diversity and regulatory mechanisms underlying complex phenotypes. In this review, we summarize recent progresses in single-cell sequencing technologies, reference cell atlas projects, and the integration of single-cell omics with population/quantitative genetics, as well as discuss how artificial intelligence and predictive perturbation modelling are reshaping single-cell research. Finally, we highlight future directions toward population-scale single-cell omics, AI-driven virtual cells/tissues, and genotype-cell/tissue-trait frameworks, which are expected to transform biological discovery, enable better design of veterinary medicines and human therapeutics, as well as accelerate sustainable farmed animal improvement and precision medicine.

records.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.

content.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has drastically enhanced healthcare diagnostics with automated disease detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent systems for clinical decision support. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of deep learning models hampers interpretability, clinical trust, and regulatory acceptance and raises concerns about data privacy and cybersecurity. This paper presents comprehensive experimental frameworks for developing and evaluating explainable AI models for secure healthcare diagnostics. The suggested model combines responsible data management, multimodal preprocessing, secure deep learning models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, and reproducible validation procedures in a single healthcare diagnostic pipeline. Methods of explaining, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and counterfactual analysis, were used to make the models more transparent and understandable for clinicians. At the same time, federated learning and differential privacy methods were used to securely manage highly sensitive patient data. Experimental evaluation has shown 96% classification accuracy, 94% sensitivity, and 95% specificity. These results were consistent in heterogeneous healthcare datasets. Compared to traditional black-box models, the explainability framework not only enhanced the interpretability of the results but also more accurately identified the regions relevant for diagnosis. Moreover, the secure federated learning architecture minimized privacy leakages without sacrificing the predictive performance and remained robust even when exposed to adversarial perturbations. An external evaluation also confirmed the reproducibility and generalizability of the protocols involved. This methodology offers a comprehensive and reliable foundation for deploying AI-powered diagnostics across multiple healthcare domains: radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, neurology, and precision medicine.

records.title: Artificial intelligence for Traditional Chinese Medicine classic formula development: a technology readiness assessment using metabolic syndrome as a case study.

content.title: Artificial intelligence for Traditional Chinese Medicine classic formula development: a technology readiness assessment using metabolic syndrome as a case study.
content.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulas, developed through millennia of clinical practice, represent a rich legacy of approximately 100,000 documented prescriptions (99,584 named formula entries in the second edition of the Dictionary of Traditional Chinese Medicine Formulas), yet on average fewer than ten new TCM products were approved annually by China's NMPA from 2013 to 2024 (77 approvals in total). The experience-based screening paradigm is misaligned with the precision medicine framework demanded by metabolic syndrome (MetS), a multi-target disorder affecting an estimated 1.54 billion adults (95% CrI 1.35-1.76) in 2023. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-encompassing knowledge graphs (KGs), large language models (LLMs), and high-throughput experimentation-has been proposed as a solution, its actual readiness for TCM development remains unclear. This review critically examines KG, LLM, and high-throughput validation technologies enabling precision phytomedicine for MetS, providing a realistic roadmap for AI-driven TCM research and development. The three technology streams exhibit asymmetric readiness. At the stream level, knowledge-graph approaches span Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3-6, large language model approaches span TRL 1-5, and high-throughput validation platforms span TRL 3-5. LLM development is limited by three TCM-specific hallucination types that lack evaluation benchmarks. KG entity recognition is the most mature component, yet reasoning is hindered by the absence of negative data, missing dose-time dimensions, and unencoded monarch-minister-assistant-envoy hierarchies. High-throughput platforms are technically feasible but remain mismatched to MetS functional endpoints-tumor-derived organoid paradigms show limited direct transferability and would require substantial adaptation. Precision phytomedicine must follow a "foundations before algorithms" sequence: institutionalize negative data, build TCM-Hallu benchmarks, establish functional-endpoint evaluation, and develop AI-assisted regulatory review. Algorithmic advances will remain in an incomplete information space until knowledge infrastructure gaps are closed.

records.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality.

content.title: Beyond Accuracy: Validation, Reproducibility, and Deployment Readiness of AI in Food Safety and Quality.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed for detecting microbial and chemical hazards in food, but laboratory accuracies are rarely reproduced in routine use. This structured narrative review examined whether reported performance is traceable, independently validated, and transferable to operational settings. Eight bibliographic databases and seven institutional routes were searched for English-language records published from January 2018 to May 2026, and we screened the records; the final corpus comprised 76 sources (53 journal articles, 9 conference papers, 2 preprints, and 12 institutional or regulatory documents). Seven primary studies supporting the quantitative evidence were appraised individually against 11 indicators, including test-set independence, external validation, and leakage control. Physical-hazard inspection and narrow-matrix spectral grading had the strongest deployment evidence, whereas microbial and chemical screening remained at laboratory or pilot scale. Among the appraised studies, the most credible estimates came from physically or temporally independent test sets, and no sensor-based study evaluated transfer to another instrument or laboratory. Deep learning showed clear advantages for image-based tasks but not consistently for small-sample spectral calibration. Adoption is limited mainly by validation design, recalibration burden, false-alarm costs, and the absence of a regulatory pathway rather than by accuracy. AI is best positioned as a screening and decision-support layer linked to confirmatory testing and human oversight.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in allergology: A Position Paper of the German Society of Allergology and Clinical Immunology (DGAKI), German Academy of Allergy, Clinical Immunology and Environmental Medicine (AeDA) and German Society of Pediatric Allergology and Environmental Medicine (GPA): Part 2.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in allergology: A Position Paper of the German Society of Allergology and Clinical Immunology (DGAKI), German Academy of Allergy, Clinical Immunology and Environmental Medicine (AeDA) and German Society of Pediatric Allergology and Environmental Medicine (GPA): Part 2.
content.abstract:
Background

Although artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing in medicine, its use in allergology remains limited. Because allergic diseases are heterogeneous and clinical, environmental, and molecular data are difficult to integrate, assessment is needed. This second part of a position paper by German allergology societies and associations, led by the German Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (DGAKI), establishes a framework for AI in allergology.

Materials and methods

The position paper is based on a narrative review and structured expert consensus and was developed in accordance with AGREE II principles. Part 2 comprises chapters 5 - 8, covering legal frameworks, ethical aspects, guiding principles for AI use, trends, and unmet needs.

Results

AI use in allergology is regulated by the EU Medical Device Regulation and the EU AI Act. Most clinical applications are classified as high-risk systems requiring strict safety, transparency, and governance standards. Physicians remain responsible for deployment, with mandatory human oversight and integration of AI-related risks into quality management and patient communication. AI raises ethical challenges beyond technical and regulatory considerations. As no broadly accepted framework exists, core biomedical and AI ethics should guide evaluation. At the same time, AI may improve access through teleconsultations, support shared decision-making, and enable more patient-centered care by reducing documentation and triage workload. AI is expected to play a pivotal role in future allergology practice and research.

Conclusion

Together with Part 1, this paper defines AI's role, outlines methodological foundations, highlights initial applications, and provides a framework for evidence-based, patient-oriented integration requiring human oversight, scientific validation, and regulatory alignment.

records.title: Assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations of artificial intelligence for depression and suicide risk: A scoping review.

content.title: Assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations of artificial intelligence for depression and suicide risk: A scoping review.
content.abstract:
Background

Depression and suicidal behavior constitute leading causes of global disease burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers promise for improving detection, intervention, and prevention, yet no comprehensive review has simultaneously mapped AI-driven assessment, intervention, and ethical considerations across both conditions.

Objective

To systematically map AI applications for depression and suicide risk across three thematic axes: (1) assessment and diagnosis, (2) conversational AI and AI-driven interventions, and (3) ethical, equity, and regulatory considerations, and to evaluate translational maturity using a novel framework.

Methods

Following JBI scoping review methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, six databases were searched from January 2020 through March 2026. Two independent reviewers screened 5079 records using a two-stage process, yielding 2844 included studies (Cohen's kappa = 0.66). Data were extracted using a standardized charting form with AI-assisted full-text analysis.

Results

Assessment/diagnosis dominated (n = 1785), with fewer intervention studies (n = 318). Large language model-related studies rose from <1% (2020-2022) to 11.1% (2025) of included studies annually. Translational Readiness Framework classification revealed 44.8% Laboratory, 49.2% Bridge, and 6.0% Clinical stage, with intervention studies showing the highest Clinical-stage proportion (16.7% vs. 5.9% for assessment). Five cross-cutting observations emerged, including an inverted evidence pyramid and persistent cross-axis integration gap (4.4%).

Conclusion

Despite technical advances, the evidence base remains concentrated at early translational stages. The proposed Translational Readiness Framework provides a structured lens for evaluating progress and guiding research prioritization. Closing the gap between laboratory promise and clinical impact requires a shift from model-centric to patient-centric research and from benchmark performance to real-world validation.

records.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for livestock genetics and breeding.
records.publisher: Journal of animal science and biotechnology

content.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for livestock genetics and breeding.
content.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern society including animal genetics and breeding which is essential for meeting global nutritional needs in supplying milk, meat, and eggs among the most complete sources of protein and micronutrients. Although animal breeding has a long history of using data-driven prediction methods, the application of modern AI approaches remains at a relatively early stage and shows substantial potential for wide-ranging applications in animal genetics and breeding. This study aims to review the current use of AI tools in livestock species across three major applications of high interest: AI-assisted phenotyping, AI-enabled dissection of complex-trait biology (focusing on AI-assisted GWAS and AI-for-omics), and AI-assisted genomic prediction. In addition, we discussed emerging methods and tools developed in human genetics that are not yet widely adopted in farm animals but may offer translational potential for future livestock studies. Looking ahead, AI breakthroughs in livestock genetics and breeding are likely to be driven by increases in data scale and resolution, enhanced computational capacities, standardized data infrastructure and benchmarking, and systematic method development and validation. From a livestock genetic improvement perspective, the key value of AI will lie in integrating AI-generated inputs, including improved phenotyping and biological insights, into practical breeding decisions through statistical modeling.

records.title: AI-Enabled Animal Behavior Analysis for Translational Pharmacology and Therapeutic Discovery.

content.title: AI-Enabled Animal Behavior Analysis for Translational Pharmacology and Therapeutic Discovery.
content.abstract: Animal behavior is a critical endpoint in preclinical pharmacology, toxicology, and therapeutic discovery, yet conventional behavioral scoring remains labor-intensive, low-dimensional, and difficult to reproduce across laboratories. Artificial intelligence (AI) can now quantify behavior from video with greater spatial, temporal, and phenotypic resolution. This review summarizes how object detection, markerless pose estimation, unsupervised behavioral segmentation, foundation models, and autonomous analysis agents are reshaping behavioral phenotyping. General-purpose object detectors rapidly localize and track animals, whereas open-source pose-estimation tools extend measurement beyond centroid tracking to body-part trajectories and fine motor patterns; paired with supervised classifiers, they have matched human scoring and exceeded some commercial systems. Technical accuracy alone does not establish behavioral construct validity or pharmacological validity. Unsupervised methods such as Motion Sequencing represent drug responses and disease-model phenotypes as structured changes in behavioral states rather than only as predefined endpoints, providing high-dimensional fingerprints of pharmacological action. Segmentation and tracking foundation models may reduce annotation burden but require validation across species, strain, sex, apparatus, and paradigm. AI agents may assist with literature review, code generation, analysis auditing, and figure production but must remain within transparent, human-supervised workflows. In behavioral pharmacology, pose estimation is established as a measurement method and emerging as a drug-effect endpoint, supervised classification and unsupervised segmentation are emerging, and foundation models and agents remain prospective. AI-enabled behavioral analysis can become a reproducible phenotyping layer for drug discovery and toxicology if researchers adopt open pipelines, rigorous validation, and reporting standards, rather than replacing one opaque measurement system with another.

records.title: Explainable fMRI decoding reveals neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal complementary to traditional analyses.

content.title: Explainable fMRI decoding reveals neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal complementary to traditional analyses.
content.abstract: Objective.Understanding how emotional arousal is represented in the brain is fundamental for elucidating affective regulation and its alterations in autism spectrum disorder. Classical neuroimaging approaches, such as the general linear model (GLM), have provided important insights into emotional processing. However, the extent to which data-driven decoding and traditional model-based analyses provide complementary information about emotional arousal remains unclear.Approach.We introduce an explainable artificial intelligence framework that combines the lightweight functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) decoder (fMRINet) with Deep Learning Important FeaTures to derive data-driven neurobiological signatures of emotional arousal. The framework enables interpretation of spatiotemporal neural contributions during emotional processing. We applied the framework to fMRI data acquired while neurotypically and autistic participants viewed naturalistic emotional videos and compared the resulting signatures with categorical and parametric GLM analyses.Main results.The framework identified distinct spatiotemporal neurobiological signatures associated with emotional arousal. Neurotypical participants engaged a distributed perceptual-limbic-prefrontal network under high arousal and frontoparietal executive regions under low arousal. In contrast, autistic participants exhibited a more spatially restricted and posterior-biased pattern under high arousal, with reduced ventromedial prefrontal and limbic contributions, while low-arousal patterns resembled typically developing, suggesting preserved executive mechanisms during low-arousal processing. The GLM analyses revealed partly convergent and partly distinct findings: categorical GLM detected no significant group differences, whereas parametric GLM identified widespread cortical-subcortical modulation in neurotypical individuals and cerebellar-restricted effects in autistic, consistent with compensatory reliance on motor-timing circuits.Significance. The proposed framework provides an interpretable, data-driven perspective on emotional processing and reveals neurobiologically plausible patterns consistent with existing literature. Together, the explainable decoding and GLM results highlight complementary aspects of emotional arousal processing, suggesting that explainable decoding approaches may provide additional insights alongside traditional model-based neuroimaging analyses.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence-Guided Surgical Planning in Glaucoma: A Systematic Review Bridging Evidence and Clinical Practice.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence-Guided Surgical Planning in Glaucoma: A Systematic Review Bridging Evidence and Clinical Practice.
content.abstract: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with diagnosis and monitoring often limited by subjectivity and variability in conventional methods. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool in ophthalmology, offering potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, predict disease progression, and guide surgical decision-making. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, with protocol registration in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (CRD420261278225). PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched from January 2010 to December 2025 using predefined terms related to glaucoma and AI. Eligible studies included original research evaluating AI algorithms for glaucoma detection, progression monitoring, risk stratification, treatment prediction, or surgical decision support. Data extraction captured study design, population, AI methodology, imaging modality, and performance metrics. Quality assessment was performed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool for diagnostic studies and qualitative appraisal for prognostic and workflow studies. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted for diagnostic accuracy studies reporting the area under the curve (AUC). Thirteen studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, with a subset contributing to the quantitative meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy, encompassing over 75,000 images and more than 10,000 patients across retrospective, prospective, longitudinal, and multicenter cohorts. AI applications are clustered into three domains: diagnosis, progression forecasting, and surgical planning. Diagnostic studies demonstrated consistently high accuracy, with pooled meta-analysis confirming a summary AUC of 0.93 (95%CI: 0.91-0.95). Multimodal approaches achieved the highest performance (AUC 0.95), outperforming single-modality fundus or optical coherence tomography systems. AI models were shown to reliably predict visual field deterioration years in advance, enabling earlier intervention. There was evidence of AI's role in surgical planning, including risk stratification, candidate selection, and structural imaging for pre-surgical assessment. Workflow integration, demonstrating the feasibility of embedding AI decision support into routine practice, was also discussed. AI has established itself as a powerful tool for glaucoma diagnosis, progression forecasting, and surgical decision-making. Quantitative synthesis confirms specialist-level diagnostic accuracy, while narrative evidence highlights emerging applications in risk stratification and clinical workflow integration. Future research should prioritise prospective multicenter validation, explainable AI frameworks, and randomised controlled trials to ensure that these technologies translate into meaningful improvements in surgical planning and long-term vision preservation.

records.title: New Insights into Cardiac Intensive Care.

content.title: New Insights into Cardiac Intensive Care.
content.abstract: In recent years, there have been significant advances in both theoretical knowledge and technological applications in cardiac intensive care, a crucial area of cardiovascular medicine. This study methodically outlines the most recent developments in the field's research, including new understandings of pathophysiological mechanisms, advancements in monitoring technology, improvements to prognostic evaluation systems, and optimization of therapeutic approaches. The article emphasizes cutting-edge advancements like artificial intelligence-assisted decision-making systems, microcirculation monitoring tools, and precision medicine approaches, which are customized to individual patient needs by combining evidence from basic research and clinical practice. Precision medicine in the cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) is described in this review as a reactive, patient-centered approach that uses real-time clinical, molecular, imaging, and hemodynamic data to customize acute therapeutic and monitoring interventions for critically ill cardiac patients with complicated, frequently multi-organ pathophysiology. Despite tremendous advancements, there are still difficulties in ensuring individualized care and converting these developments into standardized clinical procedures. In order to promote the development of standardized therapy and customized medical practice in this developing field, this thorough overview attempts to provide researchers and doctors with up-to-date information on cardiac intensive care.

records.title: Nanostructured electrode materials and flexible-substrate engineering for wearable multi-analyte biosensors in diabetes monitoring and personalized care: a comprehensive review.
records.publisher: Journal of materials science. Materials in medicine

content.title: Nanostructured electrode materials and flexible-substrate engineering for wearable multi-analyte biosensors in diabetes monitoring and personalized care: a comprehensive review.
content.abstract: This review examines the convergence of wearable biosensors and artificial intelligence (AI) in personalized diabetes care. It addresses the limitations of traditional glucose monitoring and underscores the need for continuous, multi-analyte physiological surveillance. The manuscript evaluates multi-biofluid sensing platforms, specifically those utilizing interstitial fluid (ISF), sweat, saliva, tears, and urine. ISF, an extracellular medium and a plasma ultrafiltrate, exhibits low protein content, a property that reduces sensor biofouling. ISF glucose demonstrates a strong correlation with blood glucose (R² > 0.95) and can achieve high analytical sensitivity and specificity in clinically validated systems; however, diffusion-based time lags of 5-10 min present a kinetic challenge. Consequently, AI correction is necessary to ensure real-time accuracy, which is often achieved through minimally invasive microneedle arrays. Sweat analysis allows for non-invasive, multi-parameter measurements. Nevertheless, challenges such as pH instability and analyte loss due to evaporation complicate this sensing approach. Therefore, microfluidic techniques are essential for maintaining sample stability. A primary finding indicates that clinically validated Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) systems yield substantial improvements in glycemic control, increasing Time in Range (TIR) by 10-15% and reducing the incidence of hypoglycemic events by 30-40%. AI-based predictive algorithms can forecast glucose excursions 30-60 min in advance, exhibiting an accuracy exceeding 94%. Key barriers to implementation include sensor calibration challenges, algorithmic bias, and significant healthcare equity issues. Future research should prioritize the development of multi-analyte implantable devices, leverage federated learning frameworks, and incorporate additional biomarkers to deliver continuous, multi-analyte, skin-conformal monitoring.

records.title: YOLO-geochemical integration for real-time aeolian dust monitoring: a critical review of signatures, health risks, and policy implications.

content.title: YOLO-geochemical integration for real-time aeolian dust monitoring: a critical review of signatures, health risks, and policy implications.
content.abstract: Aeolian dust is one of the most pervasive natural air pollutants, strongly influencing atmospheric chemistry, visibility, climate feedback, and human health. This review critically evaluates the integration of geochemical fingerprinting techniques and YOLO-based deep learning frameworks for real-time aeolian dust monitoring, with the overarching objective of advancing source attribution, health risk assessment, and evidence-based policy formulation in dust-prone regions. The Middle East, particularly the Qatar Peninsula, experiences recurrent dust storms that transport mineral particles and trace metals, contributing to degraded air quality, reduced solar energy efficiency, and elevated risks of respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Traditional monitoring approaches including satellite observations, ground-based measurements, and geochemical analyses such as inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive spectroscopy (SEM-EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) have improved source apportionment and compositional understanding, yet they often lack real-time detection and high-resolution spatiotemporal coverage. Emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly the You Only Look Once (YOLO) deep learning framework, offer transformative opportunities for atmospheric dust monitoring by enabling rapid, automated plume detection across multispectral and hyperspectral datasets. This review demonstrates that ICP-MS, SEM-EDS, and XRD, when applied in combination, provide robust multi-dimensional source fingerprinting: ICP-MS isotopic ratios discriminate crystal from anthropogenic contributions, SEM-EDS resolves particle-level morphology and elemental composition, and XRD quantifies mineralogical assemblages that vary systematically with source region and transport pathway. Concurrently, successive YOLO generations (YOLOv5 through YOLOv10) have achieved real-time dust plume detection with mAP values exceeding 88% on satellite and UAV imagery. The proposed multimodal YOLO-geochemical integration framework, in which YOLO-guided plume detection triggers targeted field sampling and geochemical labels iteratively retrain detection models, enables compositionally resolved, real-time exposure mapping that directly supports inhalation risk assessment against WHO PM<sub>2.5</sub> and PM<sub>10</sub> thresholds and metal-specific reference concentrations. Collectively, these findings establish a scalable, evidence-based monitoring architecture that strengthens early-warning systems, informs air quality regulation, and advances global strategies to mitigate the environmental and public health burdens of dust storms.

records.title: Patient-operated imaging for clinical assessment: regulatory and reimbursement challenges in European health systems.

content.title: Patient-operated imaging for clinical assessment: regulatory and reimbursement challenges in European health systems.
content.abstract:
Background

Patient-operated medical technologies are increasingly integrated into European care. Under EU regulation, CE marking confirms safety and performance for each specific intended use, while reimbursement requires separate demonstration of clinical and economic value. Imaging has historically differed because acquisition and interpretation are typically coupled within the same clinical encounter.

Objective

To examine patient-operated imaging for clinical assessment (POICA) as a regulatory and reimbursement boundary case under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR), and to analyse how redistribution of image acquisition to patients, while preserving clinician-led interpretation, challenges regulatory classification, liability allocation, and reimbursement models historically built around a unified professional imaging act.

Methods

We conducted a structured policy and regulatory analysis examining how patient-operated imaging interacts with existing European regulatory and reimbursement frameworks. Sources were selected based on their relevance to decentralized acquisition, clinical reliability, workflow organization, and reimbursement integration. The analysis integrates MDR and Medical Device Coordination Group (MDCG) guidance documents, usability and risk-management standards), liability principles for home-use medical devices, and the structure of European health technology assessment (HTA) and reimbursement systems. Patient-operated imaging was evaluated against precedents in which elements of technical execution moved outside institutional settings (e.g., self-testing in vitro diagnostics, home-based therapies, and remote monitoring models) to identify where existing frameworks accommodate decentralized image acquisition and where structural tensions arise.

Results

Imaging, even in structured monitoring contexts such as fertility care, requires each acquisition to meet clinical adequacy thresholds at the time of interpretation. This creates acquisition-dependent risk that cannot be mitigated through repetition alone. Under the MDR, adequacy criteria and the mechanisms ensuring them must be explicit; usability validation must demonstrate interpretative reliability rather than procedural completion. Responsibility becomes hybrid, with patients performing acquisition while clinicians retain interpretive and clinical decision-making authority. Economically, this redistribution disrupts reimbursement models built around a single bundled professional imaging act.

Conclusions

The central challenge is not regulatory authorization but maintaining clinical reliability when acquisition is decentralized. Integration into European health systems will depend on demonstrable reliability of patient-acquired images, clear allocation of responsibility, and reimbursement mechanisms capable of recognizing distributed clinical workflows, while maintaining alignment between physician incentives and high-quality care.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Obstetrics: Current Applications, Opportunities, and Clinical Implementation Challenges.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Obstetrics: Current Applications, Opportunities, and Clinical Implementation Challenges.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming obstetric practice through applications in diagnostic imaging, risk prediction, and clinical decision-making. Deep learning algorithms have achieved diagnostic accuracy comparable to that of experienced clinicians. However, gaps persist between algorithmic capability and clinical implementation. Critical challenges include limited external validation and algorithmic bias. This review examines current AI applications in obstetrics across multiple clinical domains: automated fetal biometry, structural anomaly detection, prediction of pregnancy complications, and intrapartum fetal surveillance. It highlights persistent technical, ethical, and implementation barriers. Key recommendations include multicenter validation across diverse populations, explainable AI approaches, and creating strong regulatory frameworks.

records.title: Impact, use, and implications of artificial intelligence in public health decision making by elected officials: a scoping review.

content.title: Impact, use, and implications of artificial intelligence in public health decision making by elected officials: a scoping review.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers considerable promise for strengthening governmental public health decision making by supporting rapid, comprehensive analysis of complex data. Although AI applications have been widely examined in clinical and academic settings, their use in public health agencies and policymaking remains less well understood.

Methods

This scoping review assessed how AI has been applied to support decision making by public health professionals and elected officials in both routine and crisis contexts. Using PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched PubMed, OAISTER, and Web of Science for literature published between 2014 and 2024. From 13,239 records identified, seven studies met final inclusion criteria.

Results

The identified evidence base is primarily descriptive and exploratory, with limited empirical evaluation of outcomes or effectiveness. All included studies described AI use during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on vaccination decision support, contact tracing, quarantine enforcement, and/or movement restrictions, which limits generalizability to other public health contexts and decision-making scenarios. Findings highlight a small but emerging evidence base, with most applications developed in response to emergencies rather than embedded in routine practice.

Discussion

Future opportunities for AI include advancing surveillance, communication, and resource allocation. However, critical challenges remain regarding governance, equity, and implementation. Further research is needed to evaluate AI interventions in diverse contexts and establish sustainable pathways for adoption by governmental public health agencies.

records.title: Effectiveness of telemedicine-delivered exercise interventions in older adult patients with osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effectiveness of telemedicine-delivered exercise interventions in older adult patients with osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Remote rehabilitation treatment delivered via the Internet may serve as an effective approach for managing osteoarthritis (OA). One of its primary advantages is that patients can conveniently access rehabilitation services at any time and from any location. However, there remains a lack of reliable and up-to-date systematic reviews and meta-analyses to confirm the effectiveness of this therapy in improving clinical outcomes for older adult with OA.

Purpose

Our study aims to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of the available evidence regarding the effectiveness of telerehabilitation in older adult patients with OA.

Methods

A systematic search was performed in the Medline, Web of Science, Cochrane databases, and Embase from their inception up to August 2025. Trials focusing on the effects of telerehabilitation for older adult individuals suffering from OA were included. Two reviewers, working independently, carried out the selection of studies and the extraction of data. The assessment of bias risk utilized the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool.

Results

We selected 13 randomized clinical trials, which included a total of 1,845 participants. Overall quality of the included studies was rated as moderate-to-high quality. Our findings indicate that telerehabilitation effectively alleviates pain (standardized mean difference, SMD: 0.40, 95% confidence interval, CI: 0.11 to 0.69, I 2 = 88.3%), enhances physical function (SMD: 0.61, 95% CI: 0.16 to 1.05, I 2 = 91.5%), and improves the quality of life (SMD: 0.42, 95% CI: 0.07 to 0.77, I 2 = 90.1%) in older adult individuals suffering from OA. The subgroup analysis results showed that remote exercise interventions based on APP, mobile phones, and web platforms were all effective in improving the pain levels of older adult patients with OA, and interventions with a duration of more than 3 months significantly enhanced the improvement in pain.

Conclusion

Remote exercise rehabilitation interventions have been shown to effectively alleviate pain, improve quality of life, and enhance physical function in older adult individuals with OA. This approach offers a viable alternative to traditional face-to-face exercise rehabilitation for older adult patients suffering from OA.

Systematic review registration

PROSPERO: CRD420251159586.

records.title: Early Risk Stratification of Severe Trauma in the Emergency Department: Integrating Clinical Scoring Systems, Dynamic Biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence-A Narrative Review.

content.title: Early Risk Stratification of Severe Trauma in the Emergency Department: Integrating Clinical Scoring Systems, Dynamic Biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence-A Narrative Review.
content.abstract: Severe trauma remains a major global cause of death and disability, particularly among individuals younger than 45 years. Emergency departments are the main gateway to trauma care, where rapid risk stratification guides resuscitation, surgical decision-making, intensive care admission, and resource allocation. Conventional tools, including the Revised Trauma Score, Glasgow Coma Scale, Injury Severity Score, and Trauma and Injury Severity Score, standardize early assessment but rely largely on static variables and may not capture dynamic physiological changes during resuscitation. Dynamic biomarkers offer additional biological information. Glial fibrillary acidic protein, S100B, neuron-specific enolase, serum lactate, and lactate clearance may reflect neuronal injury, tissue hypoperfusion, metabolic stress, and how effectively resuscitation is restoring perfusion. Artificial intelligence and machine-learning models can integrate vital signs, laboratory findings, imaging data, biomarkers, and demographic variables to generate individualized predictions of mortality, clinical deterioration, intensive care requirements, and complications. Recent studies suggest that some machine-learning models may outperform conventional scoring systems; however, limitations involving data heterogeneity, algorithmic bias, interpretability, external validation, privacy, and clinical workflow integration remain. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on conventional trauma scoring systems, dynamic biomarkers, and artificial intelligence-based prediction models for early risk stratification of severe trauma in emergency departments. It also examines the potential of multimodal frameworks that combine physiological, anatomical, molecular, and computational information. Although integrated prediction systems may improve accuracy and clinical decision-making, prospective multicenter validation and evidence of real-world clinical benefit are required before routine implementation.

records.title: Artificial intelligence tools for the assessment and management of dysphagia: a scoping review.

content.title: Artificial intelligence tools for the assessment and management of dysphagia: a scoping review.
content.abstract:
Objectives

To explore the existing artificial intelligence (AI) tools used in the assessment and management of dysphagia.

Design

Scoping review.

Data sources

MEDLINE (Ovid), Scopus, CINAHL (EBSCOhost), Cochrane Library, Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Evidence Synthesis, ProQuest and Google Scholar were searched for studies published between January 2000 and May 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Studies involving adults diagnosed with dysphagia that applied AI techniques for screening, diagnosis, prognosis or management were included. Non-human studies, paediatric-only studies, non-clinical simulations and studies without direct clinical application were excluded.

Methods

The review was conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, assessed full-text articles for eligibility and extracted data using a standardised data charting form. Data were synthesised using narrative synthesis.

Results

A total of 4863 records were identified, of which 27 studies met the inclusion criteria, representing 8842 participants. Most studies (21/27, 77.8%) published between 2013 and 2025 and conducted in the USA (9/27, 33.3%), South Korea (6/27, 22.2%), Japan (3/27, 11.1%) and China (3/27, 11.1%). The majority of studies (21/27, 77.8%) employed machine learning or deep learning approaches applied to videofluoroscopic swallowing studies, fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing, wearable sensor data, acoustic signals or structured clinical datasets. Most studies are prospective (8/27, 29.6%) and retrospective (7/27, 25.9%) investigations; case series (3/27, 11.1%). Only one randomised controlled trial (1/27, 3.7%) evaluated AI-based dysphagia intervention. AI applications primarily focused on screening and assessment tasks.

Conclusion

The current literature demonstrates a growing body of AI-based tools for dysphagia assessment and screening, with comparatively limited evidence for management and rehabilitation applications. Most studies highlighting the need for large-scale and multicentre studies to support safe and equitable integration of AI into dysphagia care pathways.

Trial registration number

DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/DYCE9.

records.title: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders among gig-based food delivery workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders among gig-based food delivery workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

The digital economy has spurred gig work, especially in food delivery, which grew during COVID-19. However, gig workers face occupational hazards like traffic accidents, poor ergonomics, and unsafe conditions, leading to work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Studies show high rates of back and neck pain among delivery riders due to physical strain, repetitive motions, and long hours. WMSDs reduce productivity and increase healthcare costs. This review examines WMSD prevalence, risk factors, and related issues like accidents and violence among food delivery workers.

Methods

We searched for relevant articles up to June 2025 from PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Two independent reviewers extracted data from the selected studies, including baseline information, outcomes, and prevalence of WMSDs. All data analyses were performed using R version 4.3.3.

Results
