Moderator and meta-regression analyses indicated that CHO mouth rinsing was more effective under fed conditions during aerobic exercise, when using maltodextrin solutions, rinsing for ≤10 s, and following a high-CHO meal.

Conclusions

This systematic review and three-level meta-analysis provides evidence that CHO mouth rinsing is ergogenic under fed conditions, improving both exercise and cognitive performance, though the overall certainty of evidence is low. Practical applications include its potential use as a simple, noninvasive ergogenic aid, particularly when combined with specific exercise modalities and nutritional strategies.

records.title: Optimising exercise prescription for cancer-related fatigue, lean mass, physical function and muscle strength in women with breast cancer: a systematic review with dose-response network meta-analysis.

content.title: Optimising exercise prescription for cancer-related fatigue, lean mass, physical function and muscle strength in women with breast cancer: a systematic review with dose-response network meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To systematically review and investigate the dose-response (DR) relationship of aerobic exercise (AE), resistance exercise (RE) and combined (COMB) exercise programmes on cancer-related fatigue, lean mass, physical function and muscle strength in women with breast cancer during and following primary treatment.

Design

Systematic review with DR network meta-analysis (DR-NMA; CRD42023491118).

Data sources

CINAHL, Embase, LILACS, PubMed, SciELO, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were searched from inception to 10 January 2024, with an updated search in April 2025.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials evaluating COMB, RE or AE in women with breast cancer on the four specified outcomes.

Results

64 trials (n=5156) were included. COMB was the most effective modality for improving fatigue and lean mass, and RE was the most effective for improving physical function and muscle strength. The smallest effective doses of COMB associated with significant changes in fatigue (standardised mean differences (SMD) 0.23 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.28)) and lean mass (SMD 0.30 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.38)) were 18 and 11 metabolic equivalents per week (METs.min/week), respectively. For RE, about 7-8 METs.min/week produced significant improvements in physical function (SMD 0.23 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.30)) and strength (SMD 0.24 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.29)). Fatigue benefits (SMD 0.58 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.69)) plateaued at ~1428 METs.min/week for COMB, whereas no plateau was observed for lean mass or strength across the evaluated dose range, with effects increasing throughout the available dose range.

Conclusions

COMB and RE were the most effective interventions across outcomes in women with breast cancer. Benefits for the outcomes assessed in this systematic review with DR-NMA were achieved with exercise doses as low as 10-40 min/week.

Prospero registration number

CRD42023491118.

records.title: Comparative Efficacy of Various Exercise Modes on Inflammatory Markers in Patients with Heart Failure: A Pairwise and Network Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Comparative Efficacy of Various Exercise Modes on Inflammatory Markers in Patients with Heart Failure: A Pairwise and Network Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Introduction/purpose

The aim of this systematic review with pairwise and network meta-analyses was to identify the most effective exercise mode for reducing proinflammatory markers in patients with heart failure (HF).

Methods

A systematic electronic search was carried out in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to June 2024 in English-language publications. Randomized trials investigating the effect of any mode of exercise training, including aerobic training, resistance training (RT), combined training (CT), or Tai Chi/Yoga on proinflammatory markers, including IL-6, TNF-α, or CRP in patients with HF with reduced or preserved left-ventricular ejection fraction were included. Standardized mean differences and 95% confidence intervals were determined using random-effects models for meta-analyses.

Results

A total of 21 studies involving 1022 patients with HF were included. Overall, compared with controls (CON), exercise training was significantly more effective for reducing IL-6 (SMD -0.33, 95% CI -0.56 to -0.11, P = 0.003), TNF-α (SMD -0.17, 95% CI -0.34 to -0.00, P = 0.04), and CRP (SMD -0.57, 95% CI -1.02 to -0.13, P = 0.01). Particularly, RT (SMD -0.91, 95% CI -1.32 to -0.49, P = 0.001) and Tai Chi/Yoga (SMD -0.70, 95% CI -1.22 to -0.19, P = 0.006) were the most effective modality for reducing IL-6, CT (SMD -0.44, 95% CI -0.80 to -0.09, P = 0.01) and aerobic training (SMD -0.25, 95% CI -0.49 to 0.01, P = 0.03) were the optimal modality for lowering TNF-α, and CT (SMD -1.34, 95% CI -2.28 to -0.40, P = 0.004) was the optimal modality for lowering CRP.

Conclusions

Exercise training may contribute to improvements in chronic low-grade inflammation in patients with HF. RT is likely to be the most effective exercise mode for reducing IL-6, while of the exercise modalities studied, CT was optimal for lowering TNF-α and CRP. These findings should, however, be interpreted with caution owing to heterogeneity and the limited number of studies.

records.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The aim of this overview of reviews was to determine the impact of resistance training (RT) prescription on muscle function and hypertrophy, utilizing evidence synthesis methods. It updates the American College of Sports Medicine 2009 Position Stand, "Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults."

Data sources

Ovid MEDLINE(R) ALL, Ovid Emcare, Ovid Embase, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, EBSCOhost SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science Core Collection current to October 2024.

Eligibility criteria

Eligible systematic reviews synthesized randomized trials of healthy adults (≥18 yr) who completed RT (≥6 wk; range: 6-52 wk), compared with a group that completed no exercise or an alternative RT program, and reported the change in muscle function, size, or physical performance.

Results

We synthesized data from 137 systematic reviews (>30,000 participants). Compared with no exercise (control), RT significantly improved muscle strength, size (hypertrophy), power, endurance, contraction velocity, gait speed, balance, and multiple physical function outcomes. Few RT prescription (RTx) variables affected primary adaptations. However, voluntary strength was enhanced by lifting heavier loads (≥80% one-repetition maximum), through a complete range of motion, for 2-3 sets, at the beginning of training sessions, and ≥2 sessions/wk. Muscle hypertrophy was enhanced by higher volumes (≥10 sets/wk) and eccentric overload. Power was enhanced by moderate loads (30%-70% one-repetition maximum), low-to-moderate volume (≤24 repetitions⋅sets), Olympic-style weightlifting, and power RT (fast concentric phase). Power RT enhanced physical function. Training to momentary muscle fatigue, equipment type, exercise complexity, set structure, time under tension, blood flow restriction, and periodization did not consistently impact training outcomes.

Conclusions

Healthy adults should perform progressive RT, with variable prescription consistent with our findings, to improve muscle function, size, and physical performance. Muscle strength, hypertrophy, power, and certain components of physical function can be enhanced by manipulating the RT variables highlighted.

records.title: The Effect of Strength Training on Endurance Performance Determinants in Middle- and Long-Distance Endurance Athletes: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Effect of Strength Training on Endurance Performance Determinants in Middle- and Long-Distance Endurance Athletes: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Ramos-Campo, DJ, Andreu Caravaca, L, Clemente-Suárez, VJ, and Rubio-Arias, JÁ. The effect of strength training on endurance performance determinants in middle- and long-distance endurance athletes: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 39(4): 492-506, 2025-Strength training is used to enhance endurance performance in middle- and long-distance endurance athletes. However, likely due to heterogeneity and the variety of training methodologies used, not all studies have found improvements in endurance performance with the incorporation of strength training. We aimed to review the available systematic reviews and meta-analytical evidence examining the effects of strength training on endurance performance factors in endurance-trained athletes. An umbrella review was conducted. Strength training programs were categorized into (a) maximal-strength training (>80% 1-Repetition Maximum [1RM]), (b) explosive-strength training (<80% 1RM), and (c) reactive-strength training (plyometric training). Male and/or female middle-to long-distance endurance-trained athletes were included. Variables analyzed were maximum oxygen uptake (V̇o2max), endurance performance, maximal aerobic speed or power, work and running economy, energy cost, and aerobic and anaerobic lactate thresholds. Seventeen systematic reviews were included in this umbrella review (12 with meta-analyses). Moderate to large effects were observed in all studies for running economy. Four meta-analyses examined the impact of strength training on V̇o2max, and none observed significant changes. Regarding endurance performance, 3 studies analyzed the impact of plyometric training and found small effects, except for 1 study, which found a large effect when compared with a control group. The risk-of-bias assessment revealed that most studies had low or critically low confidence levels, with issues in comprehensive literature searches, exclusion justifications, and handling publication bias. This umbrella review reveals that strength training improves endurance performance and running economy and helps maintain V̇o2max in middle- and long-distance endurance athletes. The review supports the general benefits of integrating strength training into endurance training programs.

records.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: Long-Chain Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: Long-Chain Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids.
content.abstract: Position Statement: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) presents this position based on a critical examination of the literature surrounding the effects of long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (ω-3 PUFA) supplementation on exercise performance, recovery, and brain health. This position stand is intended to provide a scientific foundation for athletes, dietitians, trainers, and other practitioners regarding the effects of supplemental ω-3 PUFA in healthy and athletic populations. The following conclusions represent the official position of the ISSN: Athletes may be at a higher risk for ω-3 PUFA insufficiency.Diets rich in ω-3 PUFA, including supplements, are effective strategies for increasing ω-3 PUFA levels.ω-3 PUFA supplementation, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), has been shown to enhance endurance capacity and cardiovascular function during aerobic-type exercise.ω-3 PUFA supplementation may not confer a muscle hypertrophic benefit in young adults.ω-3 PUFA supplementation in combination with resistance training may improve strength in a dose- and duration-dependent manner.ω-3 PUFA supplementation may decrease subjective measures of muscle soreness following intense exercise.ω-3 PUFA supplementation can positively affect various immune cell responses in athletic populations.Prophylactic ω-3 PUFA supplementation may offer neuroprotective benefits in athletes exposed to repeated head impacts.ω-3 PUFA supplementation is associated with improved sleep quality.ω-3 PUFA are classified as prebiotics; however, studies on the gut microbiome and gut health in athletes are currently lacking.

records.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Impact of Military Foot Marches on Performance-Part 1: Physical Performance.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Impact of Military Foot Marches on Performance-Part 1: Physical Performance.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Sax van der Weyden, M, Shaul, Y, Merrigan, JJ, Helton, WS, Barringer, N, Newman, K, and Martin, J. A systematic review and meta-analysis on the impact of military foot marches on performance-part 1: physical performance. J Strength Cond Res 40(5): e534-e553, 2026-Common military tasks and training require service members to have adequate physical and cognitive functioning. Foot marches are a common load carriage task for service members, potentially inducing fatigue and impairing occupational performance. The purpose of part one of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to assess the impact of military style foot marches on physical performance outcomes. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Five electronic databases were searched for studies assessing physical performance before and after a foot march at least 10 minutes in length. Three-level random effects meta-analyses were conducted using standardized mean differences (SMDs; Hedge's g). Twenty-three studies (n = 350 subjects) were included for final review. All studies were fair to good quality based on the Downs & Black checklist but had significant bias because of confounding variables when scored on the ROBINS-I tool. After adjusting for outliers and publication bias, the meta-analysis revealed significant (p < 0.05) decreases in lower-body strength (SMD = -0.45, [-0.85, -0.05]), trunk strength (SMD = -0.63, [-0.87, -0.40]), lower-body power (SMD = -0.32, [-0.63, -0.0009]), and postural stability (SMD = 0.38, [0.02, 0.70]). There was no statistical change in upper-body strength (SMD = -0.06, [-0.25, 0.12]), but in a subanalysis, shoulder strength significantly decreased (SMD = -0.22, [-0.38, -0.06]). Foot marches may decrease physical performance, with the largest decrements in trunk and lower-body strength. Alterations in strength and postural stability may lead to decreased occupational performance and increased injury risk. Commanders should be aware of potential performance decrements after a foot march and alter load, speed, and rest when possible. Holistic training programs aimed at improving aerobic and anaerobic capacity, and total body strength, may manage fatigue and reduce risk of injuries because of foot marches.

records.title: Effect of exercise snacks on fitness and cardiometabolic health in physically inactive individuals: systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Effect of exercise snacks on fitness and cardiometabolic health in physically inactive individuals: systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objectives

To evaluate the effects of brief bouts of exercise spread throughout the day, termed 'exercise snacks', on cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness, and cardiometabolic health outcomes in physically inactive adults and older adults (aged ≥65 years).

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Data sources

Seven databases were searched from inception to April 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of adults and older adults, comparing exercise snacks with non-exercising controls.

Results

11 RCTs (n=414; 69.1% women, mean age 18.7±0.8 to 74.2±5.6 years) were included. Exercise snacks were defined as structured bouts lasting ≤5 min, performed at least twice daily, ≥3 times/week, for ≥2 weeks. The interventions varied in duration (4-12 weeks), frequency (3-7 days/week) and intensity (moderate-to-vigorous to near-maximal). Exercise snacks significantly improved cardiorespiratory fitness in adults (g=1.37, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.17; p<0.005; I2=71.4 %, k=6) and muscular endurance in older adults (g=0.40, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.75; p=0.02; I2=0 %, k=4), with moderate and very low certainty of evidence, respectively. No significant effects were observed for lower limb muscular strength or cardiometabolic outcomes, including body composition, blood pressure and blood lipid profiles. High compliance (91.1%) and adherence (82.8%) rates were observed.

Conclusions

Moderate certainty of evidence indicated that exercise snacks improved cardiorespiratory fitness in physically inactive adults. However, evidence for benefits on muscular endurance in older adults was limited, and the current data do not support their effectiveness for improving other cardiometabolic health markers.

Prospero registration number

CRD42024616514.

records.title: Combined exercise training and dietary interventions versus independent effect of exercise on ectopic fat in individuals with overweight and obesity: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Combined exercise training and dietary interventions versus independent effect of exercise on ectopic fat in individuals with overweight and obesity: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression.
content.abstract:
Aim

While it is well established that reducing ectopic fat can help prevent insulin resistance in individuals with overweight or obesity, it remains unclear whether diet alone, exercise alone, or their combination is most effective in reducing specific ectopic fat depots. Therefore, the objective of this study was to investigate the effects of diet-only, and combined diet-plus-exercise interventions versus exercise only on ectopic fat reduction, and weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity.

Methods

Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus were searched for original articles, published until 1 March 2024 (no limitation on publication dates) that included diet only/or exercise and diet versus exercise alone on body weight, and ectopic fat in adults with overweight or obesity. Weighted mean differences (WMD) for body weight, liver fat, standardized mean differences (SMD) for visceral fat area (VFA), and intramuscular triglyceride (IMTG), and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were determined using random-effects models. Studies using noninvasive imaging techniques such as Computerized Tomography (CT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and hydrogen-based Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (H-MRs) for ectopic fat were included in this meta-analysis.

Results

A total of 17 studies, including 732 participants aged 24.27 to 70.5 years (309 participants with metabolic diseases, and 423 without metabolic diseases) and 38 intervention groups, met the inclusion criteria. The combined intervention of exercise and diet significantly reduced body weight compared to exercise alone [WMD = -2.85 kg, p = 0.001], with significant reductions observed in both adults with and without metabolic disease, and for interventions lasting more than 12 weeks. However, the combined intervention did not significantly reduce liver fat, VFA, or IMTG compared to exercise alone. Diet-only interventions significantly reduced body weight compared to exercise alone [WMD = -2.57 kg, p = 0.010], but did not significantly affect liver fat, VFA, or IMTG. Meta-regression indicated that weight loss was a significant moderator of the effect of combined interventions on VFA (coefficient: -0.15; p = 0.030), but not for other outcomes. Also, based on subgroup analysis by intervention duration, both exercise and calorie restriction interventions in long-term (more than 12 weeks) have been successful in decreasing VFA in adults with overweight/or obesity.

Conclusion

Combined exercise and dietary interventions are more effective than exercise alone in reducing body weight. While VFA was reduced following long-term interventions of exercise in combination with caloric restriction, our analyses showed no change in liver fat, or IMTG. Additional investigation is required to delve into the processes behind these findings and to pinpoint treatments that efficiently focus on reducing ectopic fat.

records.title: Impaired neuromusculoskeletal response to training stimuli associated with low energy availability: a systematic review.

content.title: Impaired neuromusculoskeletal response to training stimuli associated with low energy availability: a systematic review.
content.abstract:
Objective

Low energy availability (LEA) impairs musculoskeletal health, with emerging evidence of impaired neuromusculoskeletal adaptations to training. We aimed to synthesise the existing evidence examining neuromusculoskeletal responses to training stimuli among individuals with LEA.

Design

Systematic review (PROSPERO 603258).

Data sources

Six databases were searched on 4 November 2024 (total n=6399; duplicates n=2811; articles to screen n=3388). Search terms included the population and training-related exposures. Two blinded, independent reviewers screened articles using the Covidence web-based tool.

Eligibility criteria

Original articles written in English with any form of neuromusculoskeletal responses to training stimuli (premeasures and postmeasures) assessed among individuals aged ≥10 years with LEA were included. Study details, methodological quality (Physiotherapy Evidence Database, PEDro scale) and descriptive summaries with change percentages by time point and LEA status were extracted.

Results

21 studies met inclusion criteria (total participants: 536; 44% males, 56% females; PEDro: 5±2). Inconsistencies in LEA thresholds and criteria, exercise exposures and follow-up time frames precluded pooled analyses. All studies examined changes in lean muscle or fat-free mass (FFM), with seven also examining functional or activity-specific performance, and fewer concurrently examining strength, limb circumference, cellular-level or subjective neuromusculoskeletal measures. 10 studies identified that those with LEA had impaired lean mass/FFM responses (-1% to -5%), and 10 found no substantial changes over time (<1%). Six studies identified functional/sport-specific impairments over time among those with LEA (-4% to -10%). All remaining primary adaptations (strength, limb circumference, cellular-level and subjective measures) were impaired with LEA. These findings are clinically meaningful to consider, particularly for LEA-related impaired responses to rehabilitation targeting muscle hypertrophy and strength.

Conclusions

Coaches, athletes and clinicians should be aware of the evidence suggesting LEA impairs neuromusculoskeletal training responses.

records.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
content.abstract:
Background

Creatine monohydrate (CrM) is the most widely studied creatine form, demonstrating robust efficacy, bioavailability, and safety. With creatine growing in popularity, alternative formulations of creatine have been developed to target solubility and to optimize absorption pharmacokinetics (PK), as well as to reduce gastrointestinal (GI) intolerability. The purpose of the current study was to evaluate the acute effects of a novel creatine monohydrate (OptiCreatineTM; CrO) compared to CrM on serum creatine PK and GI tolerability in healthy adults.

Methods

Healthy, recreationally active adults (age: 22 ± 3 years; males n = 8, females n = 9) consumed a single 5-gram dose of CrM or CrO across two separate visits following an overnight fast, in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Venous blood samples were collected at baseline and 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, and 300 mins post-ingestion of their assigned treatment to assess serum creatine concentrations. PK parameters including peak concentration (Cmax), time to peak (Tmax), absorption rate constant (ka), elimination rate constant (kel; h-1), and area under the curve (AUC₀-T) were derived using nonlinear regression modeling. GI symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires.

Results

There was no difference in serum creatine concentrations between CrM or CrO across all participants (p = 0.707), males (p = 0.318), or females (p = 0.996) at any time point. Serum creatine increased over time regardless of treatment (p < 0.0001). No differences were observed between CrM and CrO for Cmax (mean difference ± standard deviation (MD ± SD): 7.66 ± 50.37μM; p = 0.82), Tmax (MD ± SD: -0.04 ± 0.13 h; p = 0.54), ka (MD ± SD: -0.15 ± 0.45 h-1; p = 0.51), kel (MD ± SD: 0.01 ± 0.03 h-1; p = 0.61), or AUC₀-T (MD ± SD: 22.09 ± 160.57 μM·h; p = 0.74), with no sex × treatment interactions (p ≥ 0.05). Descriptive evaluation showed similar GI symptom profiles between conditions, with low frequency and minimal severity reported across both treatments.

Conclusions

A single 5-gram dose of CrO produced similar serum creatine and PK characteristics to CrM in healthy adults. These findings support CrO as a viable delivery option, with no significant differences in acute pharmacokinetic profiles or GI tolerability compared to CrM.

records.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.

Methods

Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.

Results

Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.

Conclusions

The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

records.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
content.abstract:
Background

Healthy aging is a priority for many individuals; however, a decline in physical function and poor body composition are common age-related changes that can cause the added years from rising life expectancy to be spent in poor health. Consequently, understanding the mechanisms involved in aging has become increasingly important, including the role of phospholipids (PLs) and how age-related changes in PL content may interfere with lipid metabolism and normal functioning of the musculoskeletal system. Milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) is a bovine milk fraction rich in PLs that may have the potential to support good physical health, so that quality of life can rise alongside life expectancy.

Methods

This narrative review was based on a literature search conducted on Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus in May 2026 using the following keywords and Boolean operators: milk fat globule membrane OR MFGM AND physical function OR body composition OR older adults. Studies were included if they were randomized clinical trials (RCTs) investigating MFGM's effects on physical function and/or body composition in older adults.

Results

Findings suggest that MFGM supplementation, when consumed in conjunction with exercise, is an effective way to improve physical function in older adults, particularly among Japanese cohorts; however, changes in habitual diet in response to exercise, variable PL concentrations, and other added ingredients used in interventions may have influenced these results. In contrast, its effects on body composition appear more modest, with some studies reporting no benefits, especially when exercise was not part of the study design, or when compliance may have been a factor.

Conclusions

Beyond the combined use of supplementation and exercise, future RCTs should consistently report participant compliance and, where possible, examine MFGM as a standalone intervention to distinguish its effects from other bioactive ingredients. Greater standardization is also needed, particularly regarding PL dose. Studies should also aim to include participants from more diverse ethnic backgrounds to capture a wider range of physiological responses and improve generalizability of the findings.

records.title: Common questions and misconceptions about diets: what does the scientific evidence really show?
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Common questions and misconceptions about diets: what does the scientific evidence really show?
content.abstract: The study of diet and nutrition is often filled with numerous myths and misconceptions. A Google Scholar search of "diets health" yields over 4 million results. This review examines frequently asked questions about diets and dietary habits. These questions include the following: 1) Is a caloric surplus necessary for building skeletal muscle? 2) Is it possible to lose body mass or fat mass without caloric restriction? 3) Is intermittent fasting better than chronic caloric restriction for weight loss? 4) Are there sex differences in the response to fasting? 5) Can diet alone fulfill the macro and micronutrient needs of exercise-trained individuals? 6) Is there an ideal dietary macronutrient ratio? 7) Are most of the benefits of diets in overweight/obese individuals due primarily to the weight loss itself? 8) Do DNA-based diets induce greater fat mass loss? 9) Does eating late at night result in a gain in fat mass? 10) Are there data (i.e. observational, randomized controlled trials, etc.) on the carnivore diet? 11) Is there a diet that is best for healthy aging and longevity? 12) Is there such a thing as "superfoods?" 13) Can one consume adequate protein on a vegan diet? 14) Do high-protein diets harm the kidneys? 15) Does a greater meal frequency lead to greater weight loss? 16) Are carbohydrates more "fattening" than dietary fats? To answer these questions, we conducted an evidence-based scientific evaluation of the literature on these topics regarding the diet category.

records.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
content.abstract:
Background

Emerging evidence links movement behaviors to vitamin D status. This study investigated associations between physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep with vitamin D status and explored sex differences in these relationships.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 3195 adults (49.1 ± 17.1 years, 45.5% males) from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete data. Self-reported PA, SB, and sleep duration were assessed. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Generalized linear and logistic regression models were performed.

Results

SB was negatively associated with vitamin D levels in the whole sample (β = -0.006; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.012, -0.001) and males (β = -0.008; 95% CI: -0.014, -0.002), but not females. Sleep duration was positively associated with vitamin D among males only (β = 0.023; 95% CI: 0.003, 0.043). Meeting both PA and SB guidelines showed the strongest and most consistent association with vitamin D sufficiency, observed across the whole sample (odds ratio [OR] = 2.129; 95% CI: 1.504, 3.012), males (OR = 2.013; 95% CI: 1.021, 3.967), and females (OR = 2.214; 95% CI: 1.360, 3.605).

Conclusions

Movement behaviors demonstrate independent and joint associations with vitamin D status in US adults, with modest sex-specific patterns that warrant replication. Combined adherence to PA and SB guidelines was consistently associated with greater odds of vitamin D sufficiency across sexes.

records.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Hammond, KG, Bair, AC, Strang, AJ, Young, JC, Kruskall, LJ, Dunnick, DD, and Schilling, BK. Feasibility of heart rate-based total daily energy expenditure estimation of pararescuemen in garrison. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Pararescuemen are a group of Air Force Special Operations Forces who engage in vigorous daily training to prepare for deployment operations. This training can elicit high-energy expenditure, yet few studies have measured the energy expenditure of these airmen while at their home station (in garrison). Twelve operational pararescuemen (age: 27 ± 3 years; years of service: 5 ± 3 years) were assessed for resting energy expenditure, heart rate (HR) at rest and during initial exercise, and the HR-oxygen consumption (V̇o2) linear equation. Subjects' HR was recorded over 2 normal training days and used to estimate total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). Subjects reported an average 9 ± 2 hours of sleep per night of analysis and had an average basal metabolic rate = 82 ± 4 kcal·h-1. Average TDEE was 4,021 ± 890 kcals. Pararescuemen expend high levels of energy during routine training at their home station, similar to those of other elite military groups. Observed and reported high-energy expenditures in pararescuemen suggest further investigation into energy intake in this population to optimize performance.

records.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Payne, LKD, Varley, MC, Carey, DL, Driller, MW, and James, LP. Dimensionality reduction of full-body strength-power metrics to identify distinct strength domains in elite rugby union athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to determine the extent of shared and unique information among strength tests and to evaluate whether factors identified through exploratory factor analysis reflect distinct strength domains in professional rugby union players. Twenty professional male rugby union athletes (age 24.4 ± 3.8 years; height 186.3 ± 5.2 cm; body mass 107.6 ± 10.9 kg) completed a battery of 4 upper-body and 5 lower-body isometric, dynamic, and reactive strength tests. A total of 18 metrics were entered into exploratory factor analysis to identify distinct strength domains. Exploratory factor analysis reduced the data set into 2 upper-body domains (pressing and pulling) and 4 lower-body domains (isometric, dynamic, reactive, and relative). These domains together explained 73% of the variance in the upper-body data and 79% of the variance in the lower-body data. The isometric domain was driven by early-phase force at 100 and 200 ms, while peak force contributed less strongly. The dynamic domain was defined by heavy squat velocity, which diverged inversely from countermovement jump height, reflecting load-velocity differences. The reactive domain was shaped by contact time and countermovement depth, highlighting the role of temporal mechanics. The relative domain was defined by drop jump height and countermovement jump momentum, emphasizing the influence of body mass on ballistic force expression. Eighteen test metrics were successfully reduced to 6 distinct domains of strength in professional rugby union athletes. This framework provides a concise basis for profiling upper-body and lower-body strength to reduce redundancy and retain key information needed for training and monitoring rugby athletes.

records.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.

records.title: Efficacy of a Meta-Analysis-Recommended Immersion Protocol vs. Field-Practical Cold-Water Immersion Protocol for Performance Recovery: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Efficacy of a Meta-Analysis-Recommended Immersion Protocol vs. Field-Practical Cold-Water Immersion Protocol for Performance Recovery: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Kaji, R, Takeuchi, K, Okubo, S, and Yoshida, N. Efficacy of a meta-analysis-recommended immersion protocol vs. field-practical cold-water immersion protocol for performance recovery: A randomized crossover trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-We examined the effects of 2 cold-water immersion (CWI) protocols-15° C for 11 minutes and 10° C for 2.5 minutes-on performance recovery following exercise-induced fatigue. Fifteen male collegiate athletes completed 3 randomized crossover conditions with a 2-week washout: 15° C-11 minutes (evidence-based method), 10° C-2.5 minutes (field-practical method), and a seated-rest control. Outcomes included 20-m sprint time (T20), countermovement jump (CMJ), and Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 (YYIR2). The 20-m sprint time and CMJ were assessed before exercise (PreEx), immediately after exercise, immediately after the intervention, and at 1, 24, 48, and 72 hours postintervention, whereas YYIR2 was assessed at PreEx and at 72 hours postintervention. Physiological measures (tympanic temperature, skin temperatures, and heart rate) and perceptual measures (subjective fatigue and muscle soreness) were recorded. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol maintained T20 performance during the acute phase, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol facilitated later recovery. Countermovement jump performance transiently declined under both CWI conditions; however, a significant improvement at 72 hours occurred only with the 10° C-2.5-minute protocol. Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 performance did not differ between conditions. Thermal and cardiovascular responses varied by protocol and reflected recovery patterns. Subjective fatigue improved in both CWI conditions, whereas muscle soreness showed minimal differences. In conclusion, both evidence-based and field-practical CWI protocols enhanced recovery; however, they demonstrated distinct temporal profiles. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol supported immediate restoration, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol promoted delayed recovery. For practical applications, protocol selection should align with sport-specific demands, recovery time, and performance objectives.

records.title: Ergocycling-Based Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia Performed at Either 3,000 m or 2,000 m Similarly Impacts Overground Performance in Under-18 Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Ergocycling-Based Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia Performed at Either 3,000 m or 2,000 m Similarly Impacts Overground Performance in Under-18 Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Le Moan, D, Slawinski, J, Lecru, L, Braize, E, Brocherie, F, and Bouten, J. Ergocycling-based repeated-sprint training in hypoxia performed at either 3,000 m or 2,000 m similarly impacts overground performance in under-18 field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to compare the effects of 2 levels of hypoxic stress during ergocycling-based repeated-sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) on overground repeated-sprint ability (RSA). Fifteen highly trained under-18 male field hockey players performed a 3-week training program with 6 ergocycling-based RSH sessions (3 × 6 10-s "all-out" sprints with 20-second intraset passive recovery and 5-minute interset rest; 2 sessions per week) under moderate (MH, FiO2 14.5%, simulated altitude of 3,000 m, n = 8) or low normobaric hypoxia (LH, FiO2 16.3%, 2,000 m, n = 7). Peak (PPO) and mean power output (MPO) were recorded during each RSH session. At Pre- and Postintervention, overground sprinting horizontal force-velocity profiles and RSA test (6 × 20-m "all-out" sprints interspersed by 20 seconds) were performed. Ergocycling-based PPO (p < 0.001) and MPO (p = 0.015) improved significantly for both groups from training 1 to 6. However, overground theoretical maximal force and theoretical maximal power remained unchanged (both p > 0.377), and theoretical maximal velocity (p = 0.026) was significantly decreased for both groups. Although no significant effect (time, group, interaction) was observed for overground RSA best time and sprint decrement (all p > 0.139), RSA total time decreased (p = 0.048) in both MH and LH (-1.1 ± 2.9% and -0.9 ± 1.0%), indicating performance enhancement, irrespective of the hypoxic stress. Using moderate or low normobaric hypoxic stress during a 3-week ergocycling-based RSH intervention resulted in similar improvement during training, albeit with limited, but not negligible, transferability effect in overground performance.

records.title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Villaseca-Vicuña, R, Freitas, TT, Spyrou, K, Marín-Cascales, E, Comyns, T, Loturco, I, and Zabaloy, S. Countermovement jump performance across 10 competitive microcycles in under-18 soccer players: An analysis of delayed and long-term responses to training and official competition. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aims of this study were to (a) determine within-microcycle changes in countermovement jump (CMJ) measures (i.e., jump height, reactive strength index modified [RSImod], and eccentric peak velocity [EPV]) collected 2 days after (MD+2) and 1 day before (MD-1) the match-day across 10 weeks during the competitive period in under-18 soccer players and (b) analyze week-to-week variations in the selected CMJ-metrics collected on MD+2 across the entire mesocycle. Twelve (n = 12) under-18 academy soccer players (age: 17.5 ± 0.5 years; body mass: 71.9 ± 7.7 kg) volunteered to participate in this study. Over 10 competitive weeks, CMJ assessments were recorded on force plates at 2 key microcycle time points: MD+2 (active recovery phase at the start of the microcycle) and MD-1 (end of the microcycle). Results showed significant within-week changes in CMJ height and EPV in most of the training microcycles (p: <0.001 to 0.049) while RSImod showed significant changes in only 4 of the 10 microcycles (p: 0.001 to 0.049). Similarly, the between-week comparisons showed significant variations only in EPV and RSI (p: 0.005 to 0.049). These findings suggest that jump height might be better suited to assess within-week changes, while RSImod appears to hold greater discriminative value for detecting between-week fluctuations. Eccentric peak velocity, in turn, may provide useful information for both within-week and between-week changes in young soccer players.

records.title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Wei, X, Zhu, H, Zheng, X, Gao, Y, Huang, J, Chen, X, Vigh-Larsen, JF, Mohr, M, and Krustrup, P. Greater reductions in deceleration compared with sprint ability following repeated high-intensity exercise in male and female soccer players, but no effect on countermovement jump (CMJ) or ball-kicking performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the acute effect of repeated sprint and deceleration on the fatigue of each component (sprint vs. deceleration) and on CMJ and soccer kicking performance, and to investigate the association between deceleration ability and fatigue. Thirty-three high-level male (n = 18) and female (n = 15) college soccer players completed 10 × 15-m sprints with subsequent 5-m enforced deceleration, interspersed with 20-s recovery intervals. Sprint and deceleration performance were measured continuously during the protocol, while CMJ and kicking performance were assessed before and immediately after. Furthermore, the players' deceleration ability was measured using deceleration deficit and deceleration index. Peak deceleration had significantly higher fatigue index (FI) and decrement score (Sdec) compared with speed (p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 3.18-3.32), while no significant decline was found in CMJ or kicking performance after the repeated sprint and deceleration protocol (p > 0.05, Cohen's d = -0.06∼0.23). A significant repeated sprint and deceleration × sex interaction effect was observed in peak ball speed (p < 0.05, ηp2 = 0.149), with women showing a decrease in peak ball speed compared with their male counterparts. The deceleration index correlated with FI and Sdec of speed (r = -0.444∼-0.516, p < 0.05), and the rate of CMJ decline correlated with FI and Sdec deceleration (r = 0.530-0.549, p < 0.05). Finally, the rate of decline in kicking speed was positively correlated with the Sdec deceleration rate (r = 0.423, p < 0.05). Deceleration capacity is more prone to acute fatigue than sprint ability. In addition, repeated sprint and deceleration had a limited effect on athletic performance, but men and women showed different adjusted trends in kicking speed. Finally, players having better deceleration capacity show a smaller performance drop.

records.title: Impact of Weekly Workload Distribution on Performance in Male Soccer Players Across Competitive Levels-Scientific Hypothesis or Empirical Evidence: A Systematic Review.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Impact of Weekly Workload Distribution on Performance in Male Soccer Players Across Competitive Levels-Scientific Hypothesis or Empirical Evidence: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Lafrance, G, Dupont, G, Ahmaidi, S, and Abaïdia, A. Impact of weekly workload distribution on performance in male soccer players across competitive levels-Scientific hypothesis or empirical evidence: A systematic review. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This systematic review aimed to analyze weekly workload distribution patterns in male soccer and examine their potential effects on performance outcomes. A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases until December 2025. The analysis followed a 2-step approach: first, characterizing weekly workload distribution patterns within the microcycle, and second, examining available evidence on the potential effects of these distribution patterns on physical performance outcomes. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Forty-three studies met the inclusion criteria, with a moderate methodological quality score (5.09 ± 0.84/9). The synthesis identified a consistent weekly periodization model characterized by 3 phases: postmatch recovery (MD+1/MD+2), peak load distribution (MD-4/MD-3), and prematch tapering (MD-2/MD-1). Although this framework was common across teams, substantial observational differences in its practical implementation were reported. Regarding performance outcomes, only 2 studies (4.6%) examined the direct impact of load distribution through specific performance tests, providing limited evidence to establish clear relationships between training load patterns and physical performance. In conclusion, despite a common weekly framework, substantial differences in practical implementation across studies exist, and there is a critical lack of evidence regarding the impact of different load distribution strategies on performance outcomes. Future research should prioritize examining the relationship between weekly load distribution and performance to establish evidence-based recommendations for practitioners.

records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Relationships Between Isometric Belt Squat Force and Vertical Jump Performance Across Knee Joint Angles.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Rebelo, A, Ripley, N, Weakley, J, and Comfort, P. Relationships between isometric belt squat force and vertical jump performance across knee joint angles. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the relationships between vertical jump performance and isometric belt squat force assessed at 2 knee joint angles (120° and 90°) and to compare outcomes across age groups in male and female athletes. One hundred and twenty subjects (20.3 ± 6.5 years, 1.77 ± 0.12 m, 71.0 ± 13.3 kg) performed countermovement jumps, squat jumps, and isometric belt squat tests at 120° and 90° on dual force platforms. Between-group differences were analyzed using 1-way or Welch's analysis of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc analyses. Associations were examined using Pearson's correlations with Bonferroni-adjusted significance thresholds (p < 0.002), while omnibus tests used corrected alpha levels where applicable. Isometric belt squat net peak force demonstrated weak-to-moderate associations with jump height across tasks (r = 0.36-0.55). Associations between net force at 200 milliseconds and jump height were moderate at 90° (r = 0.45-0.52), whereas net force at 100 milliseconds showed negligible associations to jump height. Older athletes produced significantly higher absolute isometric net peak force than younger groups only at 90° knee flexion (up to ∼860 N difference), with moderate-to-large effects (g = 0.67-0.80), whereas relative net peak force did not differ between age categories. These findings indicate that the isometric belt squat can be confidently used to monitor maximal lower-limb force capacity across knee angles, with the 90° position offering greater sensitivity for distinguishing strength levels between age groups.

records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

records.title: Sleep Deprivation Selectively Alters Cellular Stress Responses During Exercise in the Heat in Young and Older Males.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Sleep Deprivation Selectively Alters Cellular Stress Responses During Exercise in the Heat in Young and Older Males.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Older adults are at heightened risk of heat-related morbidity, particularly in occupational settings where insufficient sleep and heat exposure commonly coincide. Autophagy and other proteostatic pathways are essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis during acute physiological stress; however, whether acute sleep deprivation modifies these responses during exercise-heat stress remains unknown.

Methods

Ten young (23±3 years) and 10 older (61±4 years) males completed an exercise-heat stress test following normal sleep and after 24 h of total sleep deprivation in which participants performed three 30-min cycling bouts at fixed rates of metabolic heat production (150, 200, and 250 W·m -2), each separated by 15 min rest in the heat (40°C, ~13% relative humidity). Autophagy and related cellular stress pathways were assessed before and after exercise.

Results

Sleep deprivation did not alter macroautophagy-related proteins, including LC3-II, the LC3-II/I ratio, ULK1 phosphorylation, or beclin-2 in either age group. However, p62 was reduced at end-exercise in young males following sleep deprivation (p=0.010), whereas the corresponding reduction in older males did not reach statistical significance. Sleep deprivation differentially altered proteins involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy, with LAMP-2A decreasing in young males but increasing in older males (both, p≤0.004). In older males, sleep deprivation reduced HSP90 and increased cleaved-caspase-3 and TNF-α (both, p≤0.048), indicating greater apoptotic and inflammatory signaling.

Conclusions

Our findings indicate that 24 h of sleep deprivation does not broadly alter markers of macroautophagy during exercise-heat stress but selectively modifies cellular stress pathways in older males, with distinct responses observed in young and older males.
